Stage Five — Unity and Multiplicity: Sameness, Difference, and Opposites

The objection continues: these specific features cannot take turns in one general kind either. We can answer that a general kind and its specific feature are one in their actual existence. They exist through one act of creation and are one thing outside the mind. Together, they make up a specific kind. So the qualities that belong to a specific kind in reality also belong to the specific feature that helps define it, when the mind considers that feature on its own. Since opposition is a feature of things as they exist outside the mind, it belongs directly to the specific kinds, not to their defining features considered by themselves. The opposition between two contraries depends on the specific feature of each, but their taking turns in one subject depends on the fact that they are specific kinds. To exist as a feature in a subject is a kind of existence, and only things with their own standing outside the mind can exist in that way. Defining features do not exist independently. A specific kind and its defining feature can both directly have the external qualities of the other because they are one in actual existence; this does not apply to mental qualities that belong to them only because the mind treats them as different.
Stage Five — Unity and Multiplicity: Sameness, Difference, and Opposites

Another kind of opposition is having and lacking. One side exists; the other is the absence of that thing. This absence may concern an individual, at the right time or at another time, or it may concern a kind or a general kind, whether near or broad. Examples include blindness, darkness, hair lost through a disease after it had grown, hairlessness before it grows, inability to see in a blind person, and the absence of a beard in a woman, which is possible for her kind. In each case, there is a real lack, but it depends on a subject’s ability or potential to have what is missing. That is why the lack cannot be said of something that does not exist. In the familiar definition, having is a thing’s ability to possess a feature when it chooses or when the right time comes, such as the ability to see. Lacking is the absence of this ability at a time when the subject should have it, as with a blind person—not a puppy whose eyes have not yet opened. Logicians use the broader definition given first.
Stage Five — Unity and Multiplicity: Sameness, Difference, and Opposites

Logicians also define contrary qualities simply as two things that cannot exist together in one subject. Metaphysicians add a further condition: the two must differ as much as possible. For having and lacking, they require the absence to be the loss of a feature that the subject could have at the time in question. So, in each pair, the first definition is broader than the second. But the broader definition of contrariety is called the familiar one, while the narrower is called the true one. For having and lacking, the names are reversed: the broader meaning is called the true one, and the narrower the familiar one.
Stage Five — Unity and Multiplicity: Sameness, Difference, and Opposites

Someone may object that the four kinds of opposition do not include cases such as baldness and hairlessness before hair grows, or sight and its absence in a scorpion or a tree. These are not contraries under the narrow definition, and they are not having and lacking under the narrow definition either. The reply is that the fourfold division uses the familiar, broader meaning of contrariety and the broader meaning of having and lacking. That includes these cases.
Stage Five — Unity and Multiplicity: Sameness, Difference, and Opposites

Here is a serious objection with two parts. First, in the usage of logic, contraries do not have to be two qualities that each exist in their own right. One side may be the absence of the other, as rest is opposed to motion, darkness to light, inability to speak to the ability to speak, femininity to masculinity, and oddness to evenness. Some writers say that ordinary contrariety includes true contraries and some forms of having and lacking, where the two sides take turns in one subject. But the ordinary meaning is broader still: male and female, and odd and even, do not take turns in one subject. On closer inspection, oddness and evenness belong to affirmation and denial, so they are not a separate kind of opposition.
Stage Five — Unity and Multiplicity: Sameness, Difference, and Opposites

Second, ordinary contrariety is also said to require the greatest possible difference. But then pairs such as black and red, or red and yellow, would not fit any of the four kinds of opposition, because neither pair differs as much as black and white.
Stage Five — Unity and Multiplicity: Sameness, Difference, and Opposites

Some accept that conclusion and call such pairs “mutually incompatible,” making them a fifth kind of opposition. Others answer that middle shades of color, such as red and yellow, are truly opposed in the same way as the extremes, black and white. A shade of black has both the general nature of black and its own particular degree. Compared with a weaker shade below it, it counts as black; compared with a stronger shade above it, it counts as white. Avicenna says that pure black does not itself grow stronger or weaker; rather, one shade is called darker or lighter only in relation to another. On this view, each middle shade of black is like an extreme because of the nature it shares with all black. The same holds for shades of white. So the opposition between red and yellow is true opposition insofar as one belongs to black and the other to white. Their particular colors oppose each other only indirectly. In this way, opposition between the middle shades comes back to the opposition between black and white, and there is no fifth kind.
Stage Five — Unity and Multiplicity: Sameness, Difference, and Opposites

This is the main point made by a respected later scholar. But it does not fit the earlier philosophers’ account of stronger and weaker degrees. There is another problem with it. Every thing has a nature of its own, whether or not we compare it with something else. Only a true relation depends on another thing for its meaning and existence. Colors belong to the category of quality, not relation, so each has its own nature. Contrariety belongs to things because of what they are, not because we compare one with another. The opposition between red and yellow remains even if we do not compare them with black and white. It is clearly an instance of contrariety, not of any other kind of opposition.
Stage Five — Unity and Multiplicity: Sameness, Difference, and Opposites
Stage Five — Unity and Multiplicity: Sameness, Difference, and Opposites

Those who follow Aristotle answer that true opposition belongs to the natures of black and white, apart from the particular shades. Every shade of black is opposed to every shade of white because one contains the nature of black and the other the nature of white—not because of their particular degrees. A middle shade such as red or yellow is opposed in this same way: one is taken as black and the other as white. Their particular shades differ only indirectly. So opposition between the middle colors reduces to opposition between the extremes, and no fifth kind is needed.
Stage Five — Unity and Multiplicity: Sameness, Difference, and Opposites

The earlier philosophers give a different answer. They say that the degrees of one quality oppose each other as greater and lesser, just as different amounts of one kind of quantity do. On this view, a weak shade of black and a weak shade of white oppose one another because they belong to two different kinds, regardless of their particular degrees. But a question remains: are all colors really degrees of black and white? The answer works if they are, but not if they are not. The difficulty rests on a choice of terminology, which is a small matter in the study of reason and reality.
Stage Five — Unity and Multiplicity: Sameness, Difference, and Opposites

A further point. Every existing thing has some relation to other things, whether as a cause, an effect, or in another way. It also has things that can be denied of it—at the very least, its opposite. So paired relations and affirmation and denial apply to every existing thing, including God. God is the source of all things, though He is not a father, son, or neighbor. Nor can anything escape affirmation and denial: a stone, for example, either is or is not a stone. But some things have no contrary qualities and no lack of a feature they could possess. Intelligences that do not depend on bodies cannot receive contrary qualities or lack a perfection they are able to have, because whatever is possible for them in the broadest sense is already actual. So contrariety and having-and-lacking do not apply to every thing, either generally or in each particular case.
Stage Five — Unity and Multiplicity: Sameness, Difference, and Opposites
Chapter 7 — The Opposition Between One and Many
Stage Five — Unity and Multiplicity: Sameness, Difference, and Opposites

How the one and the many oppose each other is one of the most subtle questions in the study of divine things. It has puzzled many thinkers. Only those firmly grounded in knowledge can grasp it. Their opposition is not between having a capacity and lacking it, or between affirmation and denial, because both one and many exist; neither is simply the absence of the other. Nor are they contraries. They do not differ as sharply as contraries must, since whatever number you name, you can always imagine a larger one. They also do not take turns in the same individual thing. The unity of basic matter, which can shift between being joined and divided, is only a faint shadow of unity. Multiplicity, in turn, is made up of unity.
Stage Five — Unity and Multiplicity: Sameness, Difference, and Opposites

One contrary cannot be built from anything of the other’s kind. And one and many are not opposed as a pair of relations, each defined by the other. But we can understand unity, and it can exist, apart from multiplicity. Multiplicity is many in itself because it arises from unity, not because we define it by comparing it with unity. The difference between these claims is clear. Multiplicity is related to unity because it depends on unity as its cause, not because being many is the same as being caused by unity. We see opposition between them because each excludes the other, not because one causes or depends on the other.
Stage Five — Unity and Multiplicity: Sameness, Difference, and Opposites

Also, if a thing is defined by its relation to another, the other must be defined by its relation to it too. So if multiplicity were essentially relative, unity would be as well, as happens with pairs of relations. The two would also have to depend on each other equally, both in existence and in thought. But they do not. Some people therefore say that their opposition is not intrinsic. They say it arises because unity makes up multiplicity, while multiplicity is caused by and made up of unity. But this view mixes up two different things. We understand one and many as things that cannot exist together: when one appears, it removes many, and when many appears, it removes one. Yet the unity that many removes is not the cause of that many. Many is formed through another unity, and the unity that makes up many is opposed to a different kind of unity. For example, when one continuous body is divided in two, there are two unities. One belonged to the body before it was divided; it is not part of the twoness of the two halves. The other belongs to each half and is what makes them two. There is certainly a paired relation between the new unities and the resulting twoness. But the question is: what kind of opposition holds between unity and the twoness that comes about?
Stage Five — Unity and Multiplicity: Sameness, Difference, and Opposites

If someone says, “The very idea of opposition is a kind of relation, so the opposition between one and many must be a paired relation,” we reply: the idea of opposition is a broad concept that can exist only through one of its specific kinds. Our question is which kind of opposition holds between one and many. Until we establish that, the general idea of opposition does not itself count as a specific kind of relation in the way described above.
Stage Five — Unity and Multiplicity: Sameness, Difference, and Opposites

Some people claim that one and many are not directly opposed. They argue that two opposing things must belong to the same individual thing. But unity and multiplicity do not belong to the same thing. Unity may belong to multiplicity itself, to several things that together make up one whole, or to something else that arises when multiplicity disappears and one continuous thing comes to be. In each case, the thing that bears one is not exactly the thing that bears the other. The same applies when multiplicity arises in something that was one, or in what bears it.
Stage Five — Unity and Multiplicity: Sameness, Difference, and Opposites

This argument has several problems. First, if it worked, it would also show that one and not-one, and many and not-many, are not opposed. That is plainly false. Second, the thing to which two opposing features belong does not have to be the same individual. It can belong to the same kind, or to a nearby or more distant broader kind. For example, being male or female can apply to human beings and to animals; movement and rest can apply to bodies; and good and bad can apply to things in general, however broad the case may be. If the argument were right, a thing’s defining features and necessary qualities could not oppose their negations, since the individual thing does not remain once those features disappear.
Stage Five — Unity and Multiplicity: Sameness, Difference, and Opposites

Third, even if the argument were sound, it would apply only to one particular thing and the multiplicity opposed to it, not to other kinds. Something can be one in what is said of it, in what bears the feature, or in how it relates to something else, and yet become many while remaining one in another way. Fourth, the underlying thing does not have to remain the same for every kind of opposition; this condition applies only to some kinds, such as contrary qualities. Avicenna says in The Healing that pairs of relations do not have to take turns in the same thing or belong to a shared thing. Nor must one side be able to become the other, as a cause can become an effect. Cause and effect are relations, but they do not alternate in the same thing.
Stage Five — Unity and Multiplicity: Sameness, Difference, and Opposites

Some people say that one and many are directly opposed as contraries. They argue that if we consider what the two mean, without considering that one causes or measures the other, they cannot belong to the same thing at the same time and in the same way. They say this is not the opposition of paired relations, because one and many do not depend on each other equally in existence or in thought. Nor is it either of the other two kinds, because in those, one side is the absence of the other. Unity is not the absence of multiplicity, since multiplicity is made up of unity; and multiplicity is not the absence of unity, since it depends on unity. Otherwise, a thing would cause its own absence. They also say that the claim that a contrary cannot be made up of its opposite is unsupported. But a mottled mixture of black and white can be opposed to either black or white, even though it is made up of both.
Stage Five — Unity and Multiplicity: Sameness, Difference, and Opposites

There is confusion in this argument. To call the opposition between one and many contrariety because it is not one of the other kinds is no more justified than to call it one of those other kinds. Contraries must be able to take turns in the same thing and must differ as sharply as possible. Neither condition has been shown here. The claim that a contrary cannot be made up of its opposite is not unsupported: contrary things destroy one another, so one cannot form a real nature from the other, or from both together. A mottled thing does not have one unified nature; its unity exists only in the way we imagine and describe it. So these arguments do not show that one and many fit any of the four familiar kinds of opposition. They would have to count as a fifth kind—unless we accept the familiar four kinds together with their usual conditions and results.
Chapter 1 — What a Cause Is and How Causes Are Divided

A cause has two meanings. First, it can mean something whose presence brings another thing into existence and whose absence means that the other thing is absent. Second, it can mean something on which another thing depends: without it, that thing cannot exist, but its presence alone does not guarantee that the other thing exists. In this second sense, a complete cause is enough to bring about its effect, while an incomplete cause is only one of the things the effect depends on. These include form (what makes a thing the kind of thing it is), matter (what it is made from), purpose (what it is for), and agent (what brings it about). It is wrong to say that “cause” applies to these four in unrelated senses, especially when we say that causes divide into these four kinds. The word has the same second meaning in each case: each is something on which the thing depends.

Causes are also divided into those that are parts of a thing and those that are not. A part is either what makes the thing actual—its form—or what makes it possible—its matter. A cause that is not part of the thing is either what the thing is for, its purpose, or what brings it about, its agent. Sometimes the word “agent” is used only for an outside cause, separate from the thing. What comes from within the thing is then called its element or matter. Matter, too, can be considered in two ways: as what a thing is made from, such as its element, and as what is in it, such as its arrangement or features. These are sometimes all grouped under “matter” because they share the same role of making something possible and ready to take shape. On this account, there are four causes.

Other accounts separate these kinds of matter and count five causes. Form also plays different roles toward the matter and toward the whole made from it. In its relation to matter, it is better to count form as an active cause: it works with a cause separate from matter, which helps matter take on the form it is ready to receive. We will explain this when we discuss how matter and form depend on each other. So although form gives matter its form, it is not matter’s formal cause; it is what brings that form about. This also shows why it is wrong to define an agent only as something external and separate.

Matter can also be a source of what it contains. It cannot be the source of form, since form must be in place before matter can receive it. But it can be the source of an accidental feature, because that feature first exists in something already made actual by form. Matter, considered on its own, is only a possibility. What is only possible cannot, just as such, bring anything about. Matter can, however, contribute to the nature of a whole made from matter and form, or to the existence of an accidental feature once form has made it actual.

As we have explained, matter and form can each be a direct or an indirect cause of the whole made from them, depending on how we consider them. When form is what gives a thing its basic identity, it makes matter actual, while matter is a cause of the whole. In that respect, form is a cause of the whole’s cause. But as a formal part of the whole, form is its direct formal cause. In this second role, form acts directly; nothing stands between it and the whole. When matter and an added feature together make up a particular kind of thing, matter is what bears that feature. The feature gives the whole its form, so matter is an indirect cause of the whole. But as a part of the whole, matter is its direct material cause.

In short, matter and form are direct causes of the thing because they are its parts: one is its material cause and the other its formal cause. If either one causes the whole indirectly, it does so in a different way. Matter is not its material cause in that indirect role, and form is not its formal cause in that role.

The four causes also have many connections. In one sense, the agent and the purpose cause each other. The agent brings the purpose into reality; the purpose is what the agent acts for. If someone asks why you exercise, you may answer, “To become healthy.” If someone asks why you became healthy, you may answer, “Because I exercised.” Exercise is the active cause of health, while health is the purpose of exercise. The agent causes the purpose to exist in reality, not to be a purpose or to have its particular nature. The purpose, in turn, explains why the agent acts as an agent. Matter and form also cause each other in another way, as we have noted.

Some of these causes can also be one and the same thing. As we will explain, the first cause of everything is also its purpose, both in reality and in thought. Sometimes the agent, form, and purpose are all one in nature. In a father, the source that brings the human form about in the seed is the human form itself, not some other form. What comes to be in the seed is a human form, and that is also what the seed’s development moves toward. As this form joins with matter and makes a human being, it is the form. As it begins the movement, it is the agent. As the movement reaches its end, it is the purpose. In relation to matter and the whole made from it, this one form is the form and formal cause in two ways. In relation to movement, the father’s form is the agent that starts it, while the form at which the movement arrives is its purpose, as explained in The Healing.
Chapter 2 — Why Cause and Effect Must Be Present Together

First, a cause must exist when its effect exists. An effect is possible in itself: it can either exist or not exist. A thing that must exist, or cannot exist, does not need a cause. But if it can either exist or not exist, something must tip the balance in favor of existence. That cause must be present when the effect is determined; otherwise, the effect would not depend on it at that point. And since something that does not exist cannot bring existence about, the cause must exist too. So it must be present when the effect exists.

Second, when a complete cause exists, its effect must exist as well. The leading philosophers say that if God, who must exist, brings something else into existence, He does so either by His own nature or through something that belongs to His nature. In either case, the cause is always present, so its effect should always follow. If God’s nature alone brings possible things into existence, then apart from God nothing precedes them. If He does so through an attribute that belongs to Him, that attribute is always present too. So its effect should continue for as long as God and that attribute exist.

If the cause and its permanent attribute are present but the effect is not, then God is not the full, independent cause of that effect. When the power to cause an effect is fully present, the effect either follows necessarily or still depends on something else. If it still depends on another cause, then the first cause was not enough. The second cause would also need an explanation. Either this chain goes on without end, or we reach a cause that is sufficient by itself. Wherever the complete cause is present, its effect must exist and continue for as long as that cause remains.

If God causes the effect neither by His own nature nor through an attribute that belongs to Him, then something outside Him must explain why He acts. If that outside factor itself begins to exist, we ask what caused it, as we did with the first effect. The chain cannot go on forever; it must end with God. Then the same question returns: if the factor that brings about God’s action is always present, why would its effect not continue? It makes no difference whether we call the outside factor a time, a benefit, a motive, a will, or something else.

Someone may object: God is free to choose, and He may have chosen from eternity to bring something about at one particular time rather than another. We ask: could He have chosen a different time? If not, He was forced to act at that time and was not free. Also, on that view, the act would already have to be fixed in eternity as happening at that particular time. When the act occurs, the choice to bring it about at that time ceases. The choice cannot be necessary—otherwise, it would not end then—and it cannot be part of God's own nature, for the reason just given. So it would need another cause. But this is impossible: everything besides God depends on His choice, so His choice would then depend on itself. If He could have chosen another time, something must have settled which time He chose. If that was another choice, we must ask what settled that choice, and the same question goes on without end. The first effect still needs an explanation, whether it comes from a choice or something else.

At this point, thinkers split into different groups. Some say that a free agent can choose either of two equal options without any reason favoring one. They compare this to someone fleeing a lion who sees two equally good paths and freely chooses one without a reason to prefer it.

Others say that will itself can choose one of two equal options without any further reason. They say this is simply what will does: it gives one option priority without needing a reason or motive. This ability to favor one side belongs to will by its nature, they say, just as being an animal belongs to a human being or having three angles belongs to a triangle.

Others say that God knows everything that will happen and everything that will not. What He knows will happen must happen; otherwise, His knowledge would be wrong. If only that event can occur and the other is impossible, then He must will what He knows will happen and cannot will anything else, since willing the impossible is itself impossible.

Others say that God’s actions always serve some good, even if we do not know what it is. God chooses to bring something about at a certain time because He knows that doing so then serves a good that would be lost if it happened at another time.
Others say that God’s action does not occur in eternity because of something on His side. Rather, the action itself must have a beginning, while eternity has no beginning. The two cannot go together.

This last view has a sound point, if its meaning is understood correctly. We will see this when we discuss how the world of bodies began. Others hold that God has an endless succession of new acts of will. He does one thing, then wills something else and does that, and so on without end. We will now show the problems in these views.

First, some ask why a free agent cannot choose one of two equal options without a reason. There are two replies. The first is that if we allow this, we lose the way to prove that a creator exists. That proof rests on the rule that what can either exist or not exist needs a cause. If we reject that rule, we cannot prove that God exists.

The second reply is that anything that can either exist or not exist needs a cause to settle which way it goes. We know this directly, even if we deny it in words. Until a determiner exists, neither side can become real. The determiner’s existence is not the same as our knowing that it exists. What matters is that the determiner itself is there. A thoughtful person can see this in their own experience: when the reasons for both choices seem equal, they remain still until something tips the balance.

The second view, that will can favor one side by its own nature, also fails. If both options are equal for the will, neither becomes actual without a reason. Calling this a natural power of the will does not explain anything. If the will chose the other option instead, the same supposed power would be present. Nor does it make sense to say that the will first exists without an object, then attaches itself to one. A will is always directed toward something; we cannot think of it as having no object, or as first willing just anything and only later becoming specific. When someone understands one option as better, the will turns toward it. That judgment comes before the will.

The third view says that God wills what He knows will happen. But if His knowledge that something will happen at a certain time depends on its happening at that time, then the event’s occurring at that time depends on His intention to bring it about then. If that intention, in turn, depends on His knowledge of the event, the explanation goes in a circle.

We have already shown that things that do not exist are not real things, and that essences depend on existences. You will also see that God’s knowledge brings possible things into being and comes before them; it does not follow their coming to be.

As for the fourth view—that God chooses when to act because He knows the action will serve people’s interests—we reply: the benefit that follows an act at a particular time is either bound up with the act’s very existence, or it is not. If it is, then the benefit follows whenever the act occurs. It cannot explain why the act happens at one time rather than another. If the benefit is not bound up with the act itself, then its coming from the act at this time rather than another is itself only possible and needs something to explain it. We would then have to ask what makes this time the one chosen. The only other answer is that time itself does so. But that would mean that time is something that exists, and every time is preceded by another.

If times exist in an ordered series, are possible, and come from God, then God’s act of creating must be continuous. That is the point to be proved. And how could a reasonable person accept that if the world were vastly larger, people’s interests would be ruined, or that if God had created it unimaginably earlier, those interests would be ruined too? This view also makes God’s action in general depend on something else.

As for the claim that an act does not happen earlier because it cannot happen earlier: that may make sense for particular acts and for specific natural forms that come to be in individual things. But it cannot explain creation and bringing things into existence as a whole. A possible thing needs a cause because it is possible, not because it began to exist. Nor must every act, taken as a whole, be preceded by nonexistence. The world’s possibility of coming to be has no first moment: whatever time we suppose to be the first when it could have existed is preceded by another time at which it could have existed too. A thing’s occurring at a particular time, and its being preceded by nonexistence at that time, can be understood only once time already exists. The same is true of its being in one particular place rather than another: that becomes possible only once place exists.

Some say that whether the world has always existed or began at some point, it is never free of new events and changes. One thing passes away and another comes to be. If these events depend on God, why not say that the world itself depends on Him in the same way, even if it began at some point?

The answer is that some causes prepare the way for an effect, while others actually bring it about. A preparatory cause can come before its effect because it does not bring the effect into existence; it brings the effect closer and prepares the matter to receive it. But a cause that actually produces an effect must exist alongside that effect.

Consider a heavy body falling. Its weight causes it to fall. As it falls, reaching one point prepares it to move to the next. Its weight is the cause that brings about its arrival at each point; the movement that came before prepares it for the next one. In this way, events that begin in time can depend, through a preparatory motion, on an eternal cause. That cause brings about the world in all its parts, those that came before and those that come after. Whatever event we take to be the first must have been preceded by motion and change that prepared it to receive the cause’s effect.

Here we find the starting point for another proof that God’s activity never ceases and that His giving continues to reach possible things. These events must have causes, and those causes must either be new events themselves or involve new events. Either the event comes about all at once because its producing cause begins to exist, or it comes about because a preparatory cause brings the producing cause closer to it. The first option would require an endless chain of causes and effects to exist all at once, which is impossible.

So an event comes about because it has been brought closer to its cause. That closeness comes from a preparatory cause that makes the event ready to receive the flow of existence from the giver of forms. These successive preparations cannot be separate, unconnected instants. If they were, there would be no link between one event and the next, and the earlier event would not have to lead to the later one. It could not prepare it. What remains is that the successive preparations form one continuous whole, with no actual boundaries. That whole is either a continuous existence that unfolds by its own nature, or something that depends on such a continuity, like time or motion.
We have therefore shown that events have an immediate cause.

That cause is something that continually passes and renews itself as one unbroken whole, not something made up of separate, indivisible instants. This is one of the starting points of natural philosophy. It establishes that bodily substance is continuous and cannot be made of indivisible parts. So no event can begin unless another event came before it, without any first event. Those who reject this view take one of two paths: they say that an act must be preceded by nonexistence, while eternity has no beginning, so the two cannot go together; or they say that motion and events cannot stretch back without a beginning. We will explain and answer these arguments later.
Chapter 3 — Can Something That Accompanies a Cause Come Before Its Effect?

In the sixth section of The Remarks and Admonitions, Avicenna says that something accompanying a cause that comes before its effect does not have to come before the effect too. The cause comes before its effect through causation, not through time. Something that accompanies the cause but is not itself a cause has no such priority. And if it is not prior in time or through causation, then it is not prior at all.

One scholar objects: priority is not always a matter of time or causation. There is also priority by nature: one, for example, is prior to two. So perhaps something that accompanies a cause can be prior in another way, even if it is not prior in time or as a cause.

Avicenna is not denying every other kind of priority to something that accompanies a cause. He is denying only the kind that would match the cause’s priority over its effect. By “something that accompanies a cause,” he means something that exists alongside it in relation to that causal priority. His general point is that something accompanying a thing that is prior in one way is sometimes prior in that same way, and sometimes not. What accompanies something that is earlier in time is also earlier in time. But when two things accompany a cause that comes before its effect, the second effect does not share the cause’s priority over the first effect.

A similar distinction applies to what is prior by nature. Animal comes before human being in this sense, but walking does not, even though animal and walking both come under a broader kind, such as substance. Priority by honor and by rank works in similar ways. What counts as prior can depend on the point of comparison.

Al-Rāzī raises another problem. Avicenna says that the outer sphere and the cause of the inner sphere can come from one cause and so exist together. Yet the cause of the inner sphere comes before it. The outer sphere cannot come before it, because the inner sphere’s existence and the absence of empty space within the outer sphere go together. If the inner sphere depended on the outer sphere, then so would the absence of empty space. Anything that depends on something else is possible in itself. That would make the absence of empty space possible in itself, which is absurd.

Avicenna also says in The Healing, in its discussion of heaven and earth, that intellectual beings cause their spheres to have their specific places, and are present with them in this respect. Since a cause comes before its effect, he concludes that these intellectual beings come before the elemental bodies whose places they determine.

Al-Rāzī says this passage states that what comes before an effect is prior, while the earlier passage says that what accompanies something prior is not itself prior. The two claims seem to conflict. He says that a distinction is needed, but that it is hard to find.

I see no conflict. The difference is clear. Two things are together by causation when they are both effects of one cause. Causal priority means being a cause, or having a place in the order because one is a cause. One thing cannot have two causes, but it can have two effects. So two effects exist together, and both come after their cause. Whatever accompanies one of these effects is also after the cause. But if one of two things that exist together is the cause of the other, then the other cannot also cause it; otherwise, one effect would have two causes. So there is no problem.

It is surprising that Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Tusi missed this clear distinction and offered another answer that does not work. He says that some things are together by their nature, while others only happen to be together. The word “effect” may not mean the same thing in both passages. Perhaps, then, the difference lies in what “together” means.
Chapter 4 — Why Causes and Effects Cannot Form a Circle or Stretch Back Forever

Both problems can be stated together. A chain of causes and effects could go on without end, with every cause also being an effect. If the chain has a limited number of things, it loops back on itself: a circle of two things, or of more than two. If it has no end, the chain stretches back forever. In the first case, one thing would come before itself, come after itself, and depend on itself. All of these are plainly impossible. If one thing causes another, it comes before it by one step. If the second thing also comes before the first, then the first would come before itself by two steps. The same problem grows with every added link.

Another argument is sometimes offered. Priority, posteriority, dependence, and need are relations that can be understood only between two things. The thing depended on is necessary in relation to what depends on it, while the dependent thing is possible in relation to what it depends on. But neither point proves the claim. A relation does not always require the two things to be distinct in reality; sometimes a difference in how we consider them is enough, as with the knower and what is known. And necessity does not rule out possibility in the sense of what can exist. Possibility stands to necessity as an incomplete state stands to a complete one. The two differ in how we consider them, so we should return to the argument already given.

You might object: if “a thing comes before itself” means that it comes before itself in time, this does not apply to causes. If it means that it comes before itself as a cause, then that is just the claim we are trying to prove. Saying that a thing cannot come before itself is simply another way of saying that it cannot cause itself.

I reply that “coming before” here means the kind of priority expressed by saying, “The cause existed, and so the effect existed.” A cause must exist before its effect can exist. We can say, “The hand moved, and so the ring moved.” We cannot say, “The ring moved, and so the hand moved.” This kind of priority plainly cannot hold between a thing and itself.
You might then say that a thing can cause what causes it without having to come before itself. You might offer two reasons.

First, if one thing depends on another, and that second thing depends on a third, it does not necessarily follow that the first depends on the third. Its immediate cause is enough. Otherwise, an effect could fail to follow even when its immediate cause exists.
Second, you might say that a thing’s nature causes something that, in turn, causes that thing to exist.

I reply that the dependence is unavoidable, and neither reason succeeds. Without the more distant cause, the nearer cause would not exist; without the nearer cause, the effect would not exist. That is precisely what it means to depend on something. An effect could fail to follow from its nearer cause only if that cause existed without the more distant one. As for a thing’s nature causing what causes its existence, that would seem to require the effect before its cause. But it is not the circular dependence we are discussing when the two kinds of dependence are different: form depends on matter in one respect, while matter depends on form in another.

There are many arguments against an endless chain of causes. The first is Avicenna’s argument in the Metaphysics of The Healing. He has already shown that a true cause exists together with its effect. Suppose, then, that we have an effect, its cause, and the cause of that cause. These cannot continue without end.

Consider all three together, in relation to one another. The cause of the cause is the first cause of the other two, and both stand to it as effects—one directly, the other through an intermediate cause. The effect at the end cannot be a cause of anything. The cause at the other end causes everything after it. A middle cause causes what comes after it and is itself caused by what comes before it. This remains true whether there is one middle cause or several, and whether the chain of middle causes is finite or endless.

If there are finitely many middle causes, taken together they have the same role as a single middle cause between the two ends. If there are infinitely many and so no first or last member among them, then the whole chain has the role of a middle cause: whatever part of it you take, it causes the final effect and is itself caused. The whole depends for its existence on its members. Since every member is itself an effect, the whole is an effect too. Yet the whole is also a condition for, and a cause of, the final effect. No matter how far back you trace the chain, the same holds. So there cannot be a chain of causes in which every cause is itself caused and there is no first, uncaused cause. An endless chain would be a middle with no ends, which is impossible. This, Avicenna says, is the strongest argument on this question.

The second argument is the matching argument. It applies to any existing series whose members are ordered, whether they are causes and effects, lengths and dimensions, or numbers placed in order. Suppose there were an endless series. Remove one member—or any finite number of members—from one end. You now have two series: one starts with the last member we assumed, and the other starts with the member just before it. Match the members of one series with those of the other.

If every member of the longer series matches a member of the shorter one, then the whole would equal a part of itself, which is impossible. If not every member matches, the longer series must contain a member with no match in the shorter one. The shorter series must therefore come to an end. But the longer series exceeds it only by the one member—or finite number of members—we removed. Since adding a finite number to a finite series still gives a finite series, the longer series must also be finite. This contradicts the assumption that it was endless.

The matching argument has been challenged in two ways. First, if it were sound, it would also show that numbers are finite. Compare the numbers from one onward without end with the numbers from two onward without end. Matching them would then make all numbers finite, which everyone agrees is false. It would also make God’s knowledge finite if we matched it with a smaller set that lacks one item. And it would make the motions of the heavenly spheres finite if we matched a series beginning with this revolution against one beginning with the previous revolution, though philosophers say these motions have no beginning.

Second, the argument assumes that the shorter series must come to an end if it has fewer members than the other. But endlessly doubling one gives a smaller result than endlessly doubling two, even though both go on without end. God’s power is less than His knowledge, since it concerns only what can exist, yet both are without limit. Saturn completes fewer cycles than the Moon, though philosophers say both go on without end.

The objection amounts to this: suppose every member of the longer series matches a member of the shorter one. We need not accept that the two series are equal; such a match can happen when both are endless. Even if we call them equal in this sense, it is not impossible for an endless whole and one of its shorter parts to match. We call one series larger only when it has a definite number of members beyond the other, and that need not be true of two endless series, even if one begins thousands of members later.

One answer is to say that it is self-evident that any two series are either equal or differ in size, and that the shorter one must end. The counterexamples can be answered by limiting where the proof applies.

For theologians, the proof applies to things that exist, whether they all exist together, as in a chain of causes and effects, or one after another, as with the motions of the heavenly spheres, which prepare for one another. It does not apply to numbers, because they are ideas, not things that exist on their own. Only finitely many counted things actually exist. The same applies to what God knows and what He can do: in reality, their number is finite. Their being called endless means only that there is no upper limit; beyond any number, known thing, or possible thing, there may be another.

For philosophers, the proof applies only to things that all exist at once and have an order in space or by nature, as lengths do, or as causes and effects do. So it does not apply to the motions of the heavenly spheres, which do not happen together, or to the separate members of one kind, such as rational souls, if they are endless, as some have thought. These things are not arranged in a series. The matching proof therefore does not apply to numbers, the motions of the heavenly spheres, or rational souls.

Someone might object that limiting a reasoning proof in this way admits that it fails whenever the result does not follow. I reply that the proof does not apply to the counterexamples; it applies to other cases. For theologians, things that have no actual existence can be matched only in imagination. Imagination cannot picture an endless number of things and compare them one by one. The comparison stops where the imagining stops. But if the series exists in reality, each member of one series must match a member of the other, and the mind can judge this in a single broad view without inspecting every member. For philosophers, matching in reality is possible only when things have a natural or spatial order. That is why the proof does not apply to numbers, the motions of the heavenly spheres, or rational souls.

One theologian says that both series, and the matching of their members, exist only in the mind. If the mind’s general judgment that each member must have a match is enough, then the proof applies to numbers and to things that occur one after another or all together, whether they are ordered or not. The mind can imagine the whole series. But if the mind must inspect the members one by one, the proof fails even for ordered things that exist, let alone for other cases. The mind cannot hold an endless number of things in view unless it has endless time.
I say that the difference between these cases matters. Matching is always an act of the mind and always takes place in thought. But sometimes it reflects what is real, and sometimes it does not.

In the first case, the mind needs only one broad view to judge that each member of either series matches a member of the other. The match is already present in reality, so the mind does not need to inspect each member one by one. But if the members of a series do not all exist together, or are not linked by a natural or spatial order, one broad view is not enough. The mind must picture and compare many cases, one by one.

Consider a rope. Pull one end, and the other end moves because all its parts are joined. But if those parts were merely laid side by side, without being joined, you would have to move each one separately. The same is true in the case we are discussing.
As support for this point, and as a reminder, al-Tusi, one of the most respected later scholars, writes in Naqd al-Muḥaṣṣal:

Most theologians have relied on this proof to show that the world began in time. To show that past events cannot stretch back forever, however, we need another argument. I will first present what has been said, along with the objections to it, and then give my own view.

Earlier scholars argued that past events must be finite: since each event began, the whole series began. An objection was raised that a claim about the whole does not always follow from claims about each member. They then argued that increase and decrease apply to past events, so the events must be finite. Their opponents answered with God’s knowledge and power: His knowledge includes more than His power, yet both are said to be endless.

The more careful scholars argued as follows. Take the past events, starting from this moment and going back without end. Then take them again, starting from the same moment one year ago and going back. Imagine matching the two series, with their starting points lined up as they extend into the past.

The two series cannot be equal. If they were, the events that took place between now and one year ago would both exist and not exist. The series that starts one year ago cannot be greater than the one that starts now either: what is removed from two equal things cannot be greater than either of them. So the series that starts one year ago must be smaller. For it to be smaller, it must end before the series that starts now. It would then contain only a finite number of events. The other series exceeds it only by the finite number of events from that year, so it too must be finite.
